title: Many doors to one God
hook: a man who hated Krishna merges into him, and Narada explains how
carry: one God, through the form you love
tomorrow: the universe in a toddler's mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday: or, the breath. A long breath out, a small rest at the bottom. Today Patanjali keeps opening doors, and an old story shows how many.
screen: `OR THE BREATH — A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira's great royal ceremony is underway when a king named Shishupala stands up and insults Krishna, again and again, in front of everyone. In the Mahabharata, Krishna had promised Shishupala's mother he would forgive a hundred offenses. When the count runs out, Shishupala falls. And then something stuns the hall: a light rises from the fallen man and enters Krishna. Yudhishthira can't make sense of it. A man who hated the Lord, merged into him? Later, in the Bhagavata, he asks the sage Narada how.

Narada's answer is one of the boldest passages in the tradition. What matters, he says, is a mind fixed wholly on the Lord. The cowherd women of Vraja reached Krishna through longing. King Kamsa through fear: he thought of nothing else. Shishupala and other kings through hatred. Krishna's own clan through kinship. The Pandavas through affection. Sages like Narada through devotion. So, he concludes, fix the mind on Krishna by any means. Devotees hear the obvious next step: then why not by love? Patanjali makes a quieter version of the same point. Sutras 1.35 to 1.39 each carry the little word or. Or a fine sense experience that holds the mind steady. Or the sorrowless, luminous one, which the commentator Vyasa places in the heart. Or a mind resting on someone free of attachment, a saint or a great teacher. Or what's known in dream and deep sleep. And 1.39, wide open: or by meditating on whatever you find dear. Vyasa says that isn't a loophole: once the mind steadies on what it loves, it can steady anywhere. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath both. Hindus speak of an ishta devata, a chosen deity: one God, met through the form a person loves most. That's why one home shrine has Krishna in the center and another has Shiva or the Goddess, and why one grandmother prays to Ganesha first and to Krishna longest. Some modern teachers link 1.39 to this. Not gods competing. One house, and each person comes in by the door they love.
screen: `LONGING, FEAR, EVEN HATRED.` · `WHY NOT BY LOVE?` · `1.39: WHATEVER YOU FIND DEAR.` · then, large: `ISHTA DEVATA: THE FORM YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: Today you choose the door. If you pray, your ishta devata, the form of God dear to you: Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess, Ganesha. If you don't, a soft light in the chest, the face of someone whose goodness you trust, or an image you love like the sea or a flame. Rest your attention there. When the mind wanders, come back through the same door.
Or. Five more times in sutras 1.35 to 1.39: a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, and whatever you find dear.
Your line: one God, through the form you love. Many doors, one house. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep several deities on one shrine, while each person may hold one as their ishta devata, the chosen form of God they love most; teachers often cite Yoga Sutra 1.39 for meditating on the form that is dear to you.

fork.reveal: Narada names many doors to one Lord, and 1.39 lets the mind rest on what it finds dear. Hindus call the chosen form the ishta devata.

original.note: Sanskrit iṣṭa-devatā: the chosen deity. iṣṭa means wished-for, dear: the form of God a person loves most.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hindus have many gods competing for attention.
what it means: one God met through many forms; each person may love one form most, and Patanjali's 1.39 lets the mind rest on what it finds dear.

what a scholar hears: 1.33–1.39 are upayas, 1.34–1.39 linked by va ('or'), and Vyasa says steadiness won on a chosen object carries over to others; Bhagavata 7.1 is the bhakti version: longing, fear, hatred, kinship, affection and devotion all fix the mind on Krishna.

Narada.meaning: a wandering sage and devotee who carries teachings between gods and people

Shishupala.meaning: a king who hated and insulted Krishna

ishta devata.meaning: the chosen form of God a person loves most

Patanjali.meaning: the sage traditionally credited with the Yoga Sutras

Vyasa.meaning: the classical commentator on the Yoga Sutras

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the royal consecration; Krishna's promise to forgive Shishupala a hundred offenses; his death and the light entering Krishna)
Bhagavata Purana 7.1 (Yudhishthira asks Narada how Shishupala reached the Lord; longing, fear, hatred, kinship, affection, devotion)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.35–1.39 (sense experience; sorrowless light; one free of attachment; dream and sleep; whatever is dear)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.35–1.36 (tip of the nose; the light in the heart)
